intro: These terms overlap, and each has a history of who used it and why. The fictional studies illustrate different materials and kinds of picture-making without assigning a label to an actual maker.
alt: Microsoft sees a brightly patterned painted room, a dense pencil labyrinth and a colorful sculpture made from found materials.

variants.name: Naïve art
variants.look: The sunny room combines familiar detailed objects with unusual perspective or relative scale.
variants.history: Naïve art has often described works by self-taught makers, with Henri Rousseau among the best-known examples. Appearances alone cannot establish how an artist learned.
variants.when: Study a specific artist when scale or viewpoint makes an everyday scene feel newly arranged.
variants.why: Distinctive choices about size and spacing can make the maker's attention visible across an entire picture.

variants.name: Art Brut
variants.look: Repeated pencil marks create a dense path-like pattern on a reused surface.
variants.history: Jean Dubuffet coined Art Brut in the 1940s for work he collected outside established art institutions. His collection and influence helped shape definitions that remain debated.
variants.when: Use the term when discussing the history of that collecting project or institutions formed around it.
variants.why: The collection opened attention to artists' independent choices, while the label also reflects the collector's viewpoint.

variants.name: outsider art
variants.look: The assembled work draws attention to the cork, springs and paint through repetition and gaps.
variants.history: Roger Cardinal's 1972 book helped popularize outsider art in English. The category has been used for numerous self-taught or institutionally marginal practices.
variants.when: Study an identified maker and consider how and by whom the label became attached.
variants.why: Exploring an artist's own process and materials gives a clearer entry point than assuming what a category implies.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly 3 equally wide scenes side by side in stated order in a wide 3:1 montage, separations only at vertical boundaries. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Naïve art contemporary imagined room with carefully painted plants and deliberately overlapping scale, sunny colors and flat perspective; Art Brut contextual museum panel with dense folded-pencil labyrinth on reused envelopes, no legible writing, independent imaginary work; outsider art fictional self-taught assemblage of found cork, springs and bright paint in rhythmic repeated niches on a freestanding object. These are illustrative objects, woman views from gallery edge. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
